title: The Roman Emperor Who Taxed Pee #shorts

lines.text: Did ancient Rome really tax pee? It did.
Romans collected urine from public toilets and sold it to launderers and leather makers.
Its ammonia whitened togas and tanned hides.
Around seventy A.D., Emperor Vespasian taxed it to fill the treasury.
His son Titus said that was disgusting. So Vespasian held up a gold coin and asked, does it smell?
Titus said no. Vespasian replied, yet it comes from urine.
That's where the saying, money does not stink, comes from.
So, did ancient Rome tax pee? It did, and money never smelled better.

facts.tax: vectigal urinae: first imposed by Nero, re-enacted by Vespasian around AD 70 to fill the treasury (Wikipedia, Ancient Origins)
facts.uses: urine from public urinals sold for fulling/laundering woollen togas, tanning leather (ammonia)
facts.anecdote: Suetonius, Vespasian 23.3: Titus found fault with the tax on public conveniences; Vespasian held a coin from the first payment to his nose, asked if it smelled; Titus said no; 'Yet it comes from urine'. Pecunia non olet.
facts.colosseum: begun by Vespasian c. AD 70-72, dedicated by Titus AD 80 (Britannica). Funded by Jerusalem plunder (not claimed as pee-funded).
facts.doubts: the anecdote rests on Suetonius; whether buyers paid the tax is marked citation-needed on Wikipedia, so the script only says Vespasian taxed it
